query: Analyze the existence of non-trivial cycles in the 3x+1 (Collatz) dynamical system. Using modular arithmetic and 2-adic valuation constraints from the literature, prove that any hypothetical non-trivial cycle of length k must satisfy the cycle equation x0 * (2^S - 3^k) = sum_{j=0}^{k-1} 3^{k-1-j} 2^{s_j}. Demonstrate why Steiner's bound rules out 1-cycles and 2-cycles, and establish the modern transcendence barrier via Baker's method on linear forms in logarithms.

solution:
The cycle equation is exact, but **the nonexistence of all nontrivial positive Collatz cycles remains open**. There is also a terminology correction: Steiner excluded nontrivial **one-block cycles**, and Simons extended the argument to **two-block cycles**. The number of blocks is different from the number \(k\) of odd terms. I will treat both interpretations explicitly. These historical distinctions are confirmed by [de Weger’s account](https://math.deweger.net/).

Throughout, all logarithms are natural unless a base is displayed.

Work with the accelerated map on positive odd integers,
\[
U(x)=\frac{3x+1}{2^{\nu _2(3x+1)}}.
\]
Suppose
\[
x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_{k-1},\qquad x_k=x_0,
\]
is a periodic orbit. Define
\[
a_i=\nu _2(3x_i+1)\ge1,\qquad
s_0=0,\qquad
s_j=\sum_{i=0}^{j-1}a_i,\qquad S=s_k.
\]
Thus \(k\) counts odd steps, and \(S\) counts the divisions by \(2\). The corresponding period under the unaccelerated Collatz map is \(k+S\), provided the orbit is traversed once.

The defining relations are
\[
2^{a_i}x_{i+1}=3x_i+1. \tag{1}
\]

An exponent \(a_i\) must be an **exact valuation**, not merely an exponent for which divisibility holds:
\[
\nu _2(3x_i+1)=a_i
\iff
3x_i+1\equiv 2^{a_i}\pmod{2^{a_i+1}}.
\]
Since \(3\) is invertible modulo every power of \(2\),
\[
x_i\equiv 3^{-1}(2^{a_i}-1)\pmod{2^{a_i+1}}. \tag{2}
\]
In particular,
\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
x_i\bmod 8&\nu _2(3x_i+1)\\ \hline
1&2\\
3,7&1\\
5&\ge3
\end{array}
\]
These are the elementary valuation constraints underlying the “Exact valuations and the cycle density condition” passage in [Chang’s cited preprint](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.11066).

To derive the cycle equation, set
\[
Q_r=\sum_{j=0}^{r-1}3^{r-1-j}2^{s_j},
\qquad Q_0=0.
\]
I claim that
\[
2^{s_r}x_r=3^r x_0+Q_r \qquad(0\le r\le k). \tag{3}
\]
For \(r=0\), this is immediate. If it holds for \(r\), then (1) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
2^{s_{r+1}}x_{r+1}
&=2^{s_r}(3x_r+1)\\
&=3(3^r x_0+Q_r)+2^{s_r}\\
&=3^{r+1}x_0+
  \sum_{j=0}^{r}3^{r-j}2^{s_j}.
\end{aligned}
\]
This proves (3) by induction. Substituting \(r=k\) and \(x_k=x_0\) yields
\[
\boxed{
x_0(2^S-3^k)
=
\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}3^{k-1-j}2^{s_j}.
} \tag{4}
\]

Write
\[
D=2^S-3^k,\qquad Q=Q_k.
\]
Every summand in \(Q\) is positive, so a positive cycle necessarily satisfies
\[
D>0,\qquad S>k\log_2 3,\qquad D\mid Q. \tag{5}
\]

There are useful arithmetic refinements. Both \(D\) and \(Q\) are odd: in \(Q\), only its first summand is odd. Moreover,
\[
D\equiv 2^S\not\equiv0\pmod3,\qquad
Q\equiv2^{s_{k-1}}\not\equiv0\pmod3.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\gcd(D,6)=\gcd(Q,6)=1.
\]
Thus any prime obstruction to \(D\mid Q\) occurs at primes other than \(2,3\). More precisely, integrality requires
\[
\nu_p(Q)\ge\nu_p(D)
\quad\text{for every prime }p\mid D. \tag{6}
\]
Also, reducing (1) modulo \(3\) gives
\[
x_{i+1}\equiv 2^{-a_i}\equiv(-1)^{a_i}\pmod3,
\]
so no member of a cycle is divisible by \(3\).

In fact, positivity and divisibility in (5) are sufficient to realize a prescribed valuation word, though the resulting period may divide \(k\). This is worth proving because it identifies the exact integrality obstruction.

For each cyclic rotation beginning at \(a_i\), define
\[
Q^{(i)}
=
\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}
3^{k-1-j}
2^{a_i+\cdots+a_{i+j-1}},
\]
with the empty exponent equal to \(0\) and indices read modulo \(k\). Direct expansion gives
\[
3Q^{(i)}+D=2^{a_i}Q^{(i+1)}. \tag{7}
\]
If \(D\mid Q^{(0)}\), then, because \(D\) is odd, (7) implies successively that \(D\mid Q^{(i)}\) for every \(i\). Hence
\[
x_i=\frac{Q^{(i)}}D
\]
are positive odd integers satisfying (1). Their oddness makes the valuations exact.

Therefore,
\[
\text{a prescribed positive exponent word produces an integer cycle}
\iff D>0\text{ and }D\mid Q. \tag{8}
\]

Without integrality, the same construction produces rational, \(2\)-adically admissible cycles. For example, the word \((1,3)\) gives
\[
D=16-9=7,\qquad Q=3+2=5,
\]
and
\[
\frac57
\xrightarrow{\ a=1\ }
\frac{11}7
\xrightarrow{\ a=3\ }
\frac57.
\]
Both exact valuations hold in \(\mathbb Q_2\), but neither point is an integer. This illustrates why compatible \(2\)-adic data do not by themselves establish a positive integer cycle.

Likewise, period must be distinguished from repeated notation. Suppose the exponent word is \(r\) repetitions of a block of length \(p\), with \(k=rp\). Let its affine map be
\[
F(x)=\frac{3^p x+Q_p}{2^A},
\qquad A=\sum_{i=0}^{p-1}a_i.
\]
Its multiplier \(\lambda=3^p/2^A\) is positive and unequal to \(1\), and its unique fixed point is
\[
h=\frac{Q_p}{2^A-3^p}.
\]
Since
\[
F^r(x)-x=(\lambda^r-1)(x-h),
\]
the condition \(F^r(x)=x\) forces \(x=h\), hence already \(F(x)=x\). A cycle of least odd period \(k\) must therefore have a valuation word that is not a repetition of a shorter word.

This is the global counterpart of the root-congruence constraints discussed in §7.11 of [the cited preprint](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.11066). Congruence information and least-period restrictions still leave the integer divisibility condition (8) to be resolved.

For example, the constant word \(a_i=2\) gives
\[
Q=\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}3^{k-1-j}4^j=4^k-3^k,
\]
so \(x_0=1\) for every \(k\). These words describe repetitions of the trivial fixed point, not new cycles.

The fundamental real inequality comes from multiplying (1), after division by \(x_i\), around the cycle:
\[
2^S
=\prod_{i=0}^{k-1}\left(3+\frac1{x_i}\right)
=3^k\prod_{i=0}^{k-1}\left(1+\frac1{3x_i}\right).
\]
Thus, defining
\[
\Lambda=S\log2-k\log3,
\]
we obtain the exact identity
\[
\Lambda
=\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}\log\left(1+\frac1{3x_i}\right)>0. \tag{9}
\]

Let \(M=\min_i x_i\). Because \(\log(1+t)<t\) for \(t>0\),
\[
0<\Lambda<\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}\frac1{3x_i}
\le\frac{k}{3M}. \tag{10}
\]
Also,
\[
\log_2 3
<
\frac Sk
\le
\log_2\left(3+\frac1M\right)
\le2. \tag{11}
\]
Equality at the right endpoint requires every \(x_i=1\); hence a nontrivial cycle satisfies \(S<2k\).

For a cycle restricted to the “safe” residue classes \(1,3,7\bmod8\), let \(c_1\) count the terms congruent to \(1\bmod8\). Exact valuations give
\[
S=2c_1+(k-c_1)=k+c_1.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\frac{c_1}{k}>\log_2(3/2).
\]
This establishes the cited density condition. A stationary frequency below this threshold does not, however, exclude an exceptional periodic orbit; such an exclusion requires an orbitwise argument.

Equation (10) also explains the role of continued fractions. With \(\alpha=\log_2 3\),
\[
0<\frac Sk-\alpha<\frac1{3M\log2}. \tag{12}
\]
If
\[
M>\frac{2k^2}{3\log2},
\]
then the approximation error is less than \(1/(2k^2)\). Writing \(S/k=p/q\) in lowest terms, with \(q\le k\), Legendre’s criterion implies that \(p/q\) is a continued-fraction convergent of \(\alpha\). This conclusion requires a sufficiently strong size bound; it does not follow merely from positivity of \(\Lambda\).

Cycles containing only one or two odd terms can now be excluded entirely elementarily.

For \(k=1\), equation (4) becomes
\[
x_0(2^{a_0}-3)=1.
\]
Both factors are positive integers, so
\[
x_0=1,\qquad a_0=2.
\]
This is the trivial cycle \(1\to4\to2\to1\).

For \(k=2\), suppose a nontrivial cycle exists and rotate it so that \(x_0\le x_1\). It cannot contain \(1\), so \(x_0\ge3\). Put \(a=a_0\), \(b=a_1\). Then
\[
x_1=\frac{3x_0+1}{2^a}\ge x_0
\]
implies
\[
2^a\le3+\frac1{x_0}<4.
\]
Hence \(a=1\). Equation (4) becomes
\[
x_0(2^{1+b}-9)=5.
\]
The factor in parentheses is positive. Since \(2^{1+b}>9\), it is at least \(16-9=7\), which is incompatible with the displayed equation. Thus no nontrivial cycle with two odd terms exists.

These elementary conclusions should not be confused with Steiner’s stronger theorem about one-block cycles.

To formulate that theorem, use the shortcut map
\[
T(n)=
\begin{cases}
(3n+1)/2,&n\text{ odd},\\
n/2,&n\text{ even}.
\end{cases}
\]
An \(m\)-block cycle has \(m\) increasing runs of odd terms, each followed by a decreasing run of even terms. Let \(y_i\) be its local minima, let \(q_i\ge1\) count the odd terms in the \(i\)-th run, and let \(\ell_i\ge1\) count its following even terms.

The exact run structure gives an odd positive integer \(u_i\) such that
\[
y_i=2^{q_i}u_i-1,
\qquad
2^{\ell_i}y_{i+1}=3^{q_i}u_i-1. \tag{13}
\]
Moreover,
\[
\sum_iq_i=k,\qquad
\sum_i\ell_i=S-k.
\]

For one block, \(q_0=k\), \(\ell_0=\ell\), and \(y_1=y_0=y\). Hence
\[
u(2^{k+\ell}-3^k)=2^\ell-1,
\qquad y=2^ku-1\ge2^k-1.
\]
Furthermore,
\[
e^\Lambda
=\frac{2^{k+\ell}}{3^k}
=\frac{1+1/y}{1+1/(2^\ell y)}.
\]
Therefore,
\[
0<\Lambda
<
\log(1+1/y)
<
\frac1y
\le\frac1{2^k-1}. \tag{14}
\]
This is the decisive **exponential upper bound** in the one-block argument.

A transcendence theorem supplies the opposing lower bound. For clarity, an explicit modern version can be obtained from Matveev’s theorem. Its specialization to the rational numbers \(2,3\) gives, for
\[
B=\max\{3,S,k\},
\]
\[
\left|2^S3^{-k}-1\right|
>
\exp\!\left[-H(1+\log B)\right],
\]
where one permissible constant is
\[
H=1.4\cdot30^5\cdot2^{4.5}(\log2)(\log3)
\approx5.862\times10^8.
\]
The nonvanishing hypothesis follows from unique prime factorization. See [Matveev’s original paper](https://www.mathnet.ru/php/archive.phtml?jrnid=im&option_lang=eng&paperid=314&wshow=paper); the explicit formulation used here is also recorded as [Theorem 2 in this research paper](https://math.colgate.edu/~integers/n33/n33.pdf).

Because \(2^S3^{-k}-1=e^\Lambda-1\), this implies
\[
\Lambda>
\frac12\exp\!\left[-H(1+\log B)\right]. \tag{15}
\]
Indeed, if \(0<\Lambda\le1\), then \(e^\Lambda-1<2\Lambda\); if \(\Lambda>1\), the displayed lower bound holds automatically.

From \(S\le2k\), we have \(B\le3k\). Thus there is an explicit positive constant
\[
c=\frac12e^{-H}3^{-H}
\]
such that
\[
\Lambda>c\,k^{-H}. \tag{16}
\]
The enormous constant here is chosen for transparency, not numerical sharpness. Specialized estimates for two logarithms are much stronger in applications.

Combining (14) and (16) shows that a one-block cycle must satisfy
\[
c\,k^{-H}<\frac1{2^k-1}.
\]
This fails for sufficiently large \(k\), since exponential decay eventually dominates every fixed negative power. Thus only finitely many \(k\) remain.

**The lower-bound theorem alone does not finish the exclusion.** Steiner’s theorem combines this finite reduction with continued-fraction estimates and a finite check, leaving only the trivial cycle. The structure and conclusion of that proof are described in [Simons’s paper](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/220576261_On_the_nonexistence_of_2-cycles_for_the_3x1_problem).

For two blocks, an additional estimate is necessary: one run can remain short while the other grows, so the one-block bound cannot simply be reused. Simons’s published estimates, writing \(K=k\), imply
\[
K>100,\qquad
0<\Lambda<1.19\,2^{-K/5},
\qquad K<86000.
\]
His continued-fraction argument forces a next partial quotient greater than \(3500\). But the expansion
\[
\log_2 3=[1;1,1,2,2,3,1,5,2,23,2,2,1,1,\ldots]
\]
has next partial quotients at most \(23\) for convergents with denominator below \(86000\). This is a contradiction. These estimates include the required finite exclusions and logarithmic bounds; they are Simons’s extension, not a consequence of Steiner’s bound alone. See [Lemmas 4–7 and Main Theorem 1](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/220576261_On_the_nonexistence_of_2-cycles_for_the_3x1_problem).

It remains to identify precisely why this method does not currently exclude unrestricted cycles.

First, combining only the universal bounds (10) and (16) gives
\[
c\,k^{-H}<\frac{k}{3M},
\]
or
\[
M<\frac1{3c}\,k^{H+1}. \tag{17}
\]
This is an effective restriction on the smallest cycle element. It is not a contradiction for arbitrarily large \(k\).

Second, fixing the number \(m\) of blocks provides the missing exponential upper bound, but its strength deteriorates as \(m\) grows. The following derivation makes that dependence explicit.

Assume the cycle is nontrivial, so every \(y_i\ge3\), and write
\[
\delta=\log_2 3.
\]
From (13),
\[
\begin{aligned}
y_{i+1}
&<\frac{3^{q_i}u_i}{2}\\
&=\frac12(2^{q_i})^{\delta-1}(y_i+1)\\
&\le\frac12(y_i+1)^\delta\\
&<y_i^\delta.
\end{aligned}
\]
The last inequality follows from \(y_i\ge3\) and
\[
(4/3)^\delta<2,
\]
since \(\delta(2-\delta)=1-(\delta-1)^2<1\).

Rotate the blocks so that \(y_0=M\). Iteration gives
\[
y_i\le M^{\delta^i}.
\]
Also,
\[
q_i\le\log_2(y_i+1)
\le\log_2y_i+\log_2(4/3).
\]
Therefore, setting
\[
A_m=\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}\delta^i
=\frac{\delta^m-1}{\delta-1},
\]
we obtain
\[
k\le A_m\log_2M+m\log_2(4/3),
\]
and hence
\[
M\ge
2^{\{k-m\log_2(4/3)\}/A_m}. \tag{18}
\]

The block equations also give
\[
e^\Lambda
=
\prod_{i=0}^{m-1}
\frac{1+1/y_i}{1+2^{-\ell_i}/y_{i+1}},
\]
so
\[
0<\Lambda
<
\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}\log(1+1/y_i)
<
\frac mM.
\]
Using (18),
\[
0<\Lambda
<
m(4/3)^{m/A_m}
\exp\!\left(-\frac{\log2}{A_m}k\right). \tag{19}
\]
For fixed \(m\), comparison with (16) forces
\[
\frac{\log2}{A_m}k
<
H\log k+
\log\!\left(\frac{m(4/3)^{m/A_m}}c\right).
\]
The left side grows linearly in \(k\); the right side grows logarithmically. Thus \(k\) is effectively bounded for each fixed \(m\). Since \(S\le2k\), only finitely many exponent words then remain.

This proves the fixed-block finiteness mechanism underlying the stronger bounds in [Simons and de Weger’s work](https://www.impan.pl/shop/publication/transaction/download/product/82263?download.pdf=).

But
\[
A_m\asymp\delta^m,
\]
so the exponential decay rate \((\log2)/A_m\) tends to zero as \(m\) grows. The argument supplies no uniform contradiction when the number of blocks is unrestricted. Later refinements exclude larger finite ranges—for example, [Hercher proved that a nontrivial cycle must have \(m\ge92\)](https://arxiv.org/html/2201.00406)—without resolving all \(m\).

This is the precise limitation of the logarithmic estimates used here, not a theorem that transcendence methods can never solve the problem. Likewise, finite modular exhaustion and carry constraints do not establish \(D\nmid Q\) for every nontrivial word. The finite-search qualification in the cited “Number-theoretic structure of the obstruction” passage must be retained. Even a zero-measure survivor set need not be empty.

The rigorous conclusion is therefore
\[
\boxed{
\begin{gathered}
a_i=\nu_2(3x_i+1),\qquad
s_j=\sum_{i<j}a_i,\qquad S=s_k,\\[2pt]
x_0(2^S-3^k)
=\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}3^{k-1-j}2^{s_j},
\qquad
2^S>3^k,\qquad
2^S-3^k\mid Q_k,\\[3pt]
0<c\,k^{-H}
<S\log2-k\log3
<\frac{k}{3\min_i x_i},\\[3pt]
\text{No nontrivial cycles have one or two odd terms.}\\
\text{Steiner excludes one-block cycles; Simons excludes two-block cycles.}\\
\text{Every fixed block count admits an effective finite reduction.}\\
\text{Exclusion of all nontrivial positive cycles remains open.}
\end{gathered}
}
\]
